name: Guillaume Pellicier
summary:
Guillaume Pellicier was a French prelate and diplomat who played a crucial role in the Catholic Reformation. Born into a noble family, he rose through the ranks of the Catholic Church to become Bishop of Carpentras and later Archbishop of Toulouse. Pellicier was a key figure in the Counter-Reformation, using his diplomatic skills to counter the spread of Protestantism in France.

He was appointed as the French Ambassador to the Holy See in 1556, where he played a significant role in negotiating the Treaty of Cateau-Cambrésis, which ended the Italian War of Succession. This treaty marked a significant turning point in European history, as it established a balance of power that would shape the continent for centuries to come.

Pellicier's legacy extends beyond his diplomatic achievements. He was also a prolific writer and editor, publishing several works on theology and canon law. His most notable work, 'De rectione ecclesiastica', provides valuable insights into the inner workings of the Catholic Church during this period.

One vivid example of Pellicier's impact is the establishment of the College of Clerks of the See, which he founded in 1563. This institution aimed to provide theological education and training for young clergy, helping to counter the influence of Protestantism. The college became a hub for conservative Catholics, shaping their theology and practice for generations to come.

Guillaume Pellicier died on February 4, 1568, leaving behind a legacy as one of France's most influential prelates during the Catholic Reformation.
